summary:
Entry screening at United Arab Emirates airports compares a traveller's appearance with the sex recorded in their passport. In 2025 two Israeli transgender women were held for several hours at Dubai airport, X-rayed to establish whether their genital anatomy matched the female marker in their passports, mocked by staff, refused entry and had their passports confiscated.

Refusals on the same basis are documented across a decade. In March 2022 Rachaya Noppakaroon, a Thai model and runner-up in the 2014 Miss Tiffany Universe contest, was stopped at Dubai immigration, questioned for nine hours and deported to Thailand ahead of a scheduled appearance because her passport recorded male sex. In August 2016 the trans media personality Gigi Gorgeous was detained for five hours at Dubai International Airport and her passport confiscated after officials declined to treat her gender as valid. In May 2025 the Armenian trans rights defender Lilit Martirosyan was told at Dubai that she could not enter as a transgender person while in transit, and was later permitted to leave.

Gender nonconformity is itself a federal criminal offence. Article 412(2) of the Federal Crimes and Penalties Law, in force since January 2022, punishes a man who disguises himself as a woman to enter a women-only space with up to one year's imprisonment and a fine of up to 10,000 dirhams. It replaced the broader offence in Article 359 of the 1987 Federal Penal Code, which covered wearing clothing inappropriate for one's sex in any circumstances.

Enforcement under that regime has turned on presentation rather than conduct. On 9 August 2017 the Singaporean transgender woman Nur Qistina Fitriah Ibrahim and her companion Muhammed Fadli Abdul Rahman were arrested at Yas Mall in Abu Dhabi while wearing jeans, sneakers and long-sleeved shirts, charged under Article 359 and Abu Dhabi's local public-morals offence, and sentenced on 20 August 2017 to one year's imprisonment and a fine without legal representation. They were held for nearly three weeks in a cell designated for effeminate detainees, where guards shaved their heads and discarded Ibrahim's hormone pills, before their sentences were converted to deportation and they were deported on 28 August 2017. Other transgender women and feminine-appearing people were held in the same facility solely for looking feminine in mixed-gender public places, including while wearing men's clothing or work uniforms.

Further documented cases include the arrest in Dubai in December 2013 of two Brazilian transgender women who called police about prejudice they had witnessed in a nightclub and were themselves detained for imitating women until March 2014, fined 10,000 dirhams and ordered deported; a 2005 Abu Dhabi Police raid on a hotel gathering that arrested 26 young men alleged to have cross-dressed, of whom 12 were convicted, 11 to five-year sentences and one to a year, with initial reports that some were ordered to accept hormone treatments in exchange for lighter sentences; arrests and deportations of foreign residents in 2020 for clothing deemed inappropriate for their sex; and a June 2011 Dubai police campaign targeting transsexuals and boyat.

Consensual same-sex conduct is criminalised under Article 409(1)(b) of the Federal Crimes and Penalties Law, Federal Decree-Law No. 31 of 2021, which came into force on 2 January 2022 and carries a minimum of six months' imprisonment with no maximum prescribed. Under Article 409(5) proceedings may be brought only on the complaint of a spouse or guardian, who may withdraw it at any time. Because same-sex marriage is not recognised and civil guardianship ends at 18, no eligible complainant exists for consensual conduct between adult men, whereas a married woman's husband or, under the Islamic wali concept, an unmarried Muslim woman's father or male relative can qualify, so prosecution of women remains possible where such a complainant exists. The law prescribes no death penalty for consensual same-sex conduct, and no arrests or prosecutions for consensual same-sex sexual activity are documented since at least 2015 as of 2026, consistent with United States Department of State human rights reporting.

No UAE law or policy prohibits discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation, gender identity or expression, or sex characteristics, and no legal gender recognition is available. No LGBTQI+ support or advocacy organisation operates openly anywhere in the country; in Dubai no formal LGBTQ organisations or nightclubs exist, and a nightclub that ran a special night for the community was shut down by the government. LGBTI organisations cannot register.

Sex reassignment surgery is severely restricted to limited circumstances that are highly regulated by the state. Gay conversion practices are not prohibited or discouraged by any law or regulation. Reports document mistreatment in detention, including beatings and forced rectal examinations amounting to torture, as consequences of suspected or established same-sex conduct.

A Brazilian trans woman held in the country since September 2022, arrested after refusing a police-requested toxicology test, accused the consulate of negligence in April 2023; the record does not show her release.

The UAE does not recognise same-sex marriage.
tangentialFactors:
The documented entry refusals and transit detentions all occurred at Dubai or Abu Dhabi airports. The record contains no account from any other emirate's entry point, so the pattern is established at the two largest international gateways rather than measured across the country's other crossings.

Public-decency and dress charges have also been used against gay and bisexual men, which indicates the wider enforcement environment a gender-nonconforming visitor enters. In 2012 two Indian men received six months each plus deportation for consensual sex in a public bus-station toilet, a British man and another man received three-year sentences plus deportation for drunken public sex, a Belgian man received one year plus deportation in June 2012, and a police raid on 21 March 2012 broke up a gathering of 30 men. In October 2017 a Scottish tourist arrested for public indecency after touching a man's hip had charges dropped following intervention by the ruler of Dubai.

Censorship extends to trans-specific content. The Media Regulatory Office banned Spider-Man: Across the Spider-Verse in June 2023 over a scene showing a Protect Trans Lives transgender flag, banned Pixar's Lightyear in June 2022 for depicting a same-sex relationship, and the Arabic children's comic Majid came under investigation in 2022 with an edition withdrawn over dialogue using the word مثلي. The country's sole internet provider blocks sites on dating, marriage and LGBTQ issues, and Amazon removed 150 search terms including lgbtq, pride and closeted gay from its UAE site in June 2023 under threat of penalties.

Officials have publicly declared that there is no room for homosexual and queer acts in the UAE. The Outright International country overview underlying parts of this assessment was last updated on 12 March 2026.

Residents have no route to legal gender recognition, and no UAE law or policy protects them from discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation, gender identity or expression, or sex characteristics.

Article 409(5) of the Federal Crimes and Penalties Law structures prosecution through a spouse or guardian complainant. Since civil guardianship ends at 18 and same-sex marriage is unrecognised, no eligible complainant exists for consensual conduct between adult men, while for women a husband or, under the Islamic wali concept, a father or male relative can qualify. Article 412(2) applies to a man disguising himself as a woman to enter a women-only space, but enforcement records show charges brought against transgender women and feminine-appearing people for their appearance in ordinary mixed-gender public places.

Sex reassignment surgery is available only in limited, highly state-regulated circumstances. Involuntary medical and psychological treatment, including hormonal therapies and detention for forced psychological treatment, has occurred in connection with suspected or established same-sex conduct, and gay conversion practices are not prohibited or discouraged by any law or regulation.

No LGBTQI+ support or advocacy organisation can operate openly or register, and no formal LGBTQ organisations or nightclubs exist in Dubai; a nightclub's special community night was shut down by the government. Community-facing content is censored through the internet provider, the Media Regulatory Office and platform-level term blocking.

Resident-facing enforcement includes a June 2011 Dubai police campaign targeting transsexuals and boyat, and arrests and deportations of foreign residents in 2020 for clothing deemed inappropriate for their sex.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the anatomy check reported at Dubai airport in 2025 rests on a written screening instruction or on ad hoc practice by individual officers is not sourced here; the record contains accounts of the outcome, not the procedure's legal basis.

The record does not state whether a passport bearing an updated gender marker changes the outcome of entry screening, or how a visitor whose documents are consistent with their presentation is assessed. No sourced rule on document markers or visa issuance for transgender applicants appears in this inventory.

The outcome of the Brazilian trans woman's detention, reported in April 2023 after she had been held since September 2022, is unresolved in this record; no later status is sourced.

No aggregate figure for the number of transgender travellers refused entry, detained or deported is available, so the frequency of the pattern cannot be quantified from these sources. The cases above are the documented instances, not a measured rate.

Whether Article 412(2) has been charged against visitors since the 2017 Abu Dhabi convictions is unresolved; the most recent documented entry refusal in this record is from May 2025 and the most recent documented prosecution of a visitor for gender presentation is from August 2017.
